grounded_facts: Berlin stands firm against St Anne's attempts to find inconsistency in his testimony.
Berlin rejects St Anne's version of events and insists he has been consistent and truthful throughout.
memories.memory_text: I was told that St Anne tried to challenge my account, but I stood firm and told them I already gave the truth — I wasn't going to let them find some inconsistency that doesn't exist.

grounded_facts: St ANNE questions Berlin about quitting smoking and drinking, implying health and memory issues.
memories.memory_text: I was there when St ANNE questioned Berlin about quitting smoking and drinking, implying he had memory and health issues—I heard her mention memory blackouts and how too much booze can be dangerous.

grounded_facts: St ANNE informs Berlin that a janitor was present at the institute the night of the incident, undermining Berlin's account of events.
memories.memory_text: I was told by St ANNE that a janitor was in the institute that night — that the flashlight, the footsteps, and the moving elevator were all him, not me, and that the storm caused the door to swing and knock me down.

grounded_facts: Berlin proposes a new theory: the janitor saw him with a gun, panicked, hit him with a door, took the gun, and shot Ross in confusion.
memories.memory_text: I was told Berlin's theory that the janitor saw him with a gun, panicked, hit him with the door, took the gun, and shot me in confusion.

grounded_facts: A formal police interrogation of Berlin by St ANNE regarding the events at the institute.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed the formal police interrogation of Berlin by St ANNE, where she referenced the exact time I was shot and the janitor's call, making it clear the timeline was locked in by the recording.

grounded_facts: St ANNE uses timing evidence to disprove Berlin's claim that the janitor could have shot Ross.
memories.memory_text: I witnessed St ANNE use timing evidence from the recording to show the janitor couldn't have shot me, because he was on the phone with police at the exact time I was shot.

grounded_facts: St ANNE reveals that Ross switched to channel 8, allowing the police to record the entire incident, including the exact time of the shooting.
memories.memory_text: I was told that I switched to channel 8, which allowed the police to record the entire incident, including the exact time of the shooting.

grounded_facts: St ANNE challenges BERLIN's loyalty and emotional bonds by questioning the nature of his friendship with Ross, attempting to isolate him psychologically.
memories.memory_text: I was told that I wasn't much of a friend and that I humiliated someone, and I heard the question about whether I shot my best friend, all meant to make me doubt my loyalty and our bond.

grounded_facts: St ANNE plays a recording of the incident that implicates BERLIN in the shooting of his best friend Ross, causing emotional devastation.
memories.memory_text: I heard my own voice on that recording—me calling out to John, begging him to stop—and then the shots. I didn't know it would be played, but I realize now it was me he was trying to warn before everything went wrong.

grounded_facts: TAYLOR breaks the silence after St ANNE leaves, suggesting BERLIN accept the deal, while simultaneously expressing personal dislike.
memories.memory_text: I heard Taylor break the silence after St Anne left, telling Berlin to take the deal while making it clear he didn't like him.

memories.memory_text: I was involved in a police interrogation where I was questioned about shooting my friend, heard offers and denials of deals, and was confronted with personal questions about my drinking, all while trying to hold my ground.

memories.memory_text: I stared at Berlin in that empty room, and for a moment he wasn't him—he was the man I lost, standing in the same spot, breathless, silent, just like before the wind carried everything away.
I think that's when I heard her call him John—standing there, wanting to feel the snow on my face, and that name just surfaced, like it had been buried.
I asked if Amber was dead, and when Berlin said yes, the silence after felt heavier than before—like something final had settled.
I turned into the spray, laughing as the cold sea hit my face—it felt like the best thing anyone had ever invented, and I knew Berlin was feeling it too, right beside me.

I told Berlin that Ross had spoken about him—his age, his nervous tick, how he’s chubby—and when I said fifty-seven, he didn’t seem angry, just amused, like it was a game I wasn’t meant to know the rules to.

The van came up fast behind us, jumping in and out of view with the dunes, and when it overtook, I knew—immediately—that it was the Hollow Car, the one that sounds hollow, and I said so, voice tight, before it vanished into the dark.
I reached for his hands, and for a moment I was so glad to see him—but then I felt it, each second stretching heavier, knowing this was the last time.
I wanted it to be a surprise, setting the table with the candles and the Forget-Me-Nots, waiting for him to come home.

I knew before he said anything—he walked in too quiet, and the silence between us had already changed. When I asked if he wanted coffee, it wasn't just to fill the space, but to delay the moment just a little longer.
I could feel the ache in my chest, standing there at the sink—knowing he was going to say goodbye, and not wanting to face it, not even to myself.
I looked up from the sink and for just a second—there he was, a tall, strange face staring in, so close to the glass, and then gone.
I remember handing him the forget-me-nots at the door, and how he took my hand before bringing it to his lips—then we kissed, clumsy and close, like we didn’t quite know how to say goodbye.

I closed the cupboard after stacking the last plate, and then I noticed something was off in the apartment—there was a sound I couldn’t place. I followed it to the bedroom and saw the curtains moving, fluttering in the dark, and realized the window was half open, though I didn’t remember opening it.
I checked the water temperature and turned the tap on when it was too cold. I silenced the indicator. Then I turned and saw someone in the dark.
A flash—dazzling light hit me, and I turned, certain I’d heard something, but there was only darkness and the feeling of being watched, then nothing.

I was on the phone with Mr. Goodridge, and I could feel my voice shaking as I said I couldn't find the number—he kept pressing, and I just repeated that I’d call tomorrow, even though I already knew I wouldn’t.
I remember the warmth of Berlin’s lips in the moonlight, how the music wrapped around us like it was the only thing breathing in the room.
The phone rang while we were kissing. When it was answered, I heard Berlin say, 'I gotta tell you, Margie. You are Mrs Santa Claus.'
I asked Margie when John divorced and what his ex-wife was like—Suzanne, a model who left him—and how it broke him, how he couldn’t handle losing her.
I wondered if John would like me in the red dress, standing there in the heels Margie made me try, feeling unsure but wanting to know what he’d think.

I felt the weight of the mascara brush on my lashes, the drag of lipstick pulled carefully across my mouth—each stroke a step I couldn’t take back, standing there while MARGIE adjusted the red sequins over my shoulders.
I saw Ross’s eyes widen when he turned—his mouth opened before he said it—'Wow'—and for a second, I wasn’t sure if it was mockery or real, but the word hung there like it meant something.
I said I couldn't walk in these shoes, and my voice sounded small, like it was coming from somewhere far away.
I felt his hands on my legs, the clip of my stockings releasing, and when he kissed me, I helped him with my brassiere—like I was both there and not.
I remember the weight shifting on the bed, and then the silence where his breath used to be—just the wind, and something metallic clicking, loud, like it was inside my head.
I saw my own body on the wall, naked in the bathroom, blown up like some trophy among all those other girls—he must have watched me without me knowing.
I remember asking John why I couldn't stay with him, my voice quiet but insistent, holding on to his hand like it was the only solid thing left.
I said I was going back to the institute, even after John told me no—not now—and Margie offered to have me stay with her instead.
I whispered, 'I need the number for a cab, please,' my fingers still touching the phone book, the silence after the words feeling heavier than before.
I stepped onto the porch and called out, 'John? Is that you?'—the fog was thick, and the only answer was the rattle of crows, nothing more.

I bumped into a brown Chevrolet I hadn’t seen before, checked it quickly, and then froze—something clattered, maybe in the garage, and I asked again, 'John, is it you?' not knowing where the sound came from.

I felt my fingers brush the wardrobe door as I passed, and in that instant, the mirror showed someone behind me—completely in black, a man I hadn’t heard, hadn’t known was there—then his gloved hand clamped down on my wrist like a trap.
He took my hand and ran the blade over my palm, then closed my fingers around the handle. He said he cut my friend's head off with it. I couldn't move. Tears fell down my face.

memories.memory_text: I was already walking toward the infill when Travis told me the guy from L.A. had gone down there ahead of me—waiting for me, like he had any right to be on my dump, poking around before I even arrived.
I saw the blood on the raincoat and heard Trimble say they cut his throat—knew right away it wasn't a clean suicide, not with that kind of cut.
I asked Berlin where the knife was—no weapon at a scene like that means someone took it, probably that kid hanging around who saw more than he let on.
I crouched in the garbage, shone my light into the sack, and saw it—a severed hand. I said, 'You're right. It's a fucken hand,' then handed the flashlight over.
I was soaked and freezing, scanning the trash under that goddamn rubber cape, when someone shouted about a brassiere with blood on it. All I could say was 'Oh, shit.'

After Berlin said it was good to be with me, I cracked that I’d rather lie down with the derelict than stay another minute—and for once, he almost smiled. Then I told him, 'Glad you finally made it, Bro.'

I pulled out the champagne, ready to celebrate, but Margie shot me down—said it was Californian, not French, like I claimed, and suddenly even that small thing felt like another thing I couldn't get right.

I told Berlin to watch my lips and not get into it—shut him down hard when he started asking about 'frozen' and digging into the hand. That case wasn't ours, never was, and I wasn't gonna let him drag it back to life.

Berlin asked about the 'Jennifer' case, and I told him it was an unsolved mess—half a million down the drain, and Taylor’s the one who worked it. I didn’t say it straight, but he knows Taylor blames him for the promotion.
I told Berlin about waking up with my heart pounding so hard I could've made love with my left tit — same as him, back when I was chained to cigarettes.
When he said a dollar wasn't worth quitting for, I upped it to fifty — and he took the bet, just like that.
I looked up from the papers and caught Citrine passing by—smoke in the air, sleeves rolled—and said I wanted to give that fat lady a lie-detector test, how she’s making my life a misery.
I asked Berlin what he thought the case was, and when he started obsessing over the Zippo again, I called him out—told him he couldn't stop clicking, picking, worrying. Same as back in L.A.
Berlin suddenly sprinted through the rain. He shouted that the victim was blind—because of the beeping traffic light and Braille on her fingertips.

My Chevy tore up the valley, sunlight flashing off the snow before the bend swallowed me, and I aimed it at that dead-eyed Victorian thing with fifty windows and a clock tower—like some goddamn asylum no one told me about.

I remember standing there, ready to punch that smug look off Goodridge’s face when he acted like Amber just walking out was no big deal — a blind girl leaving with some unknown guy and he’s giving us lectures about independence.
I mouthed 'F.I.F.T.Y' slow and clear, watching Berlin stiffen without turning—Helena walking right through it, clueless, while he pretended the whole thing wasn't happening.
I leaned in close and whispered it straight into his ear—'Fifty fucken dollars, O.K.'—then followed up right after with 'Fifty of em. And I want em now,' just as the elevator doors opened.

I was elbow-deep in the engine, trying to keep the old boat running, when Berlin started yelling over the noise about a ballistics match in San Diego—like that was supposed to mean something to me while I'm covered in oil and my son's watching the revs.
I asked Berlin why the FBI didn’t put the cases together, since they worked on 'Jennifer' for months.
I told Berlin no—flat out. He wants to tear apart the Blind Institute, but walking in with his homicide and my mayor scandal? We’d lose everything. I couldn’t back him, even if part of me wanted to.

I was just trying to keep my head down, pouring a drink, and then Serato walks in saying Emerson passed the polygraph with flying colors—like it was nothing. I remember the words hitting me: 'Oh my God Mother's shit. Are we in it?'
I remember stepping out of the mist with Berlin, the cheap Christmas lights glowing overhead, and when he started whining about God, I shut him down—no God, just asses at kicking height.

I told Berlin he's dragging L.A. around like an addiction, just like I used to—pissed off and running on fumes, living off the vitamins in cigarettes. If there's a body under the snow, fuck it, let someone else dig it up.

I waved my empty glass at the bar, asking for another drink while telling Berlin he's getting too far into the element—she's blind, lonely, and he's a nice guy to have around, but emotional involvement screws everything up.
I asked Berlin who he thought did it, even though he gave me that look like I was an idiot for asking.
After he went off about the bad man out there, I didn't know what to say—just asked if I could help, and he didn't even know what to do with that.
I ripped a beer from the crate and handed it to Berlin, told him not to thank me—Margie’s the one who stocked the place.
I grabbed a six-pack and tossed it to Berlin, told him to give it to some old guy in a cell and say happy Christmas from me.

I told Berlin his gut's getting soft and his body's falling apart—mine's no better, gut in its fifties, balls in their sixties, feet in the eighties. Joked about it like it was nothing, even though the cold and the booze make every ache feel real.

Berlin snapped at me to hit the wipers—saw a light, thought it was a flashlight on the fourth floor. The second he said it, I was locked in, adrenalin kicking, everything suddenly loud and fast after all that stillness.

I'm huddled against the wall, sleet slashing sideways, and the damn flashlight gives out—glows like a dying tangerine before going dark. Right when I'm trying to check Helena's place and make sure Berlin's alright, the light dies, and all I can hear is this noise upstairs, something moving.

I was getting torn apart by the wind, batteries almost dead, and still no answer from Berlin on the radio—tried every channel, kept asking if he heard me, but nothing. So I said fuck it, light or no light, I'm going up.

A blinding flashlight hits me in the face from someone rushing down, I call out it's me, Freddy, but then I see the glint of a small gun at the edge of my vision—next thing I know, two shots tear into me, one nearly taking my hand off, the other slamming me in the gut.
I tried to speak, but the blood filled my throat—nothing came out, just heaving, like an old bull elephant choking on its last breath.

I dunno, I daren't go in there - just about get her wired up, and the fucking mayor walks in - mad as hell - what are we doing fucking with his staff? We should be out chasing major violators ..
